source: Open Science Collaboration (2015) Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science
finding: 100 psychology experiments replicated with high power and original materials. Most failed the significance test, and effects shrank by half.
numbers: 97 of 100 originals significant; 35 of 97 (36%) replications significant in same direction. Mean original effect size .403 (SD .188); replications about half. 47% of original effects inside replication 95% CI. 39% subjectively rated replicated. Pooled original plus replication: 68% significant.
quote: Replication effects were half the magnitude of original effects
limits: Vote counting is crude: replications near the threshold count as failures. Originals are inflated by selection. Only three journals, year 2008.
agent_relevance: One published pass is weak evidence. Expect the true effect to be smaller than the first estimate and demand a held-out re-run (G3).

source: Open Science Collaboration (2015) Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science (by area and moderators)
finding: Replication success was predicted by the strength of the original evidence, not by who ran the replication.
numbers: Significant in original direction: JPSP 7/31 (23%), JEP:LMC 13/27 (48%), Psych Science 7/24 (29%). Mean replication power .92 (median .95), so about 89 positives were expected if the originals were true; 35 were seen.
limits: Correlational. Team expertise and self-rated replication quality did not explain failure.
agent_relevance: Weight a result by the strength of its first evidence, not by how confident the producing model sounds.

source: Camerer et al. (2018) Evaluating the replicability of social science experiments in Nature and Science 2010-2015
finding: 21 high-profile social science experiments replicated at about five times the original sample. 13 replicated.
numbers: 13 of 21 (62%) significant in same direction. Mean relative effect size 50%; for the replicated studies 74.5%, for the 8 that failed 0.3%. Stage 1 sample about 3x original, stage 2 about 6x. 90% power to detect 75% of the original effect. True-positive relative effect size estimated at 71%.
quote: we successfully replicated 13 out of 21 findings
limits: Small set of studies. Even true effects look inflated in the originals.
agent_relevance: High-power re-tests recover real effects but at about half to three quarters of the first size. Size a test for a smaller effect than the first one seen.

source: Camerer et al. (2018) prediction markets and survey beliefs
finding: Peers predicted replication outcomes well before data came in.
numbers: Average prediction market belief of replicating about 60.6%, close to the observed 62% rate. Beliefs strongly correlated with outcome.
limits: Only 21 studies. Forecasters were researchers, not models.
agent_relevance: A cheap prior can steer which tests to spend on. For ideas, G8 still says judge by running.

source: Klein et al. (2018) Many Labs 2: variation in replicability across samples and settings
finding: 28 findings, each run in about half of 125 samples from 36 countries, total N 15,305. About half replicated.
numbers: 15 of 28 (54%) significant same direction at p<.05; 14 (50%) at p<.0001. Median Cohen d original 0.60, replication 0.15. 21 of 28 (75%) effects smaller than original, 7 (25%) larger.
limits: Slate design: each lab ran part of the protocols. Original authors sometimes disputed the replication conditions.
agent_relevance: Failure to replicate is not mainly about sample or place. Suspect inflated originals before invoking an unnamed moderator.

source: Klein et al. (2018) Many Labs 2: heterogeneity and moderators
finding: Hidden moderators (culture, setting, mode) explained little of the variation.
numbers: Q-test significant heterogeneity in 11 of 28 effects (39%). Only one effect had tau above .20; nine others about .10. Very little heterogeneity due to task order, lab vs online, or WEIRD vs less-WEIRD (exploratory).
limits: Moderator tests were exploratory.
agent_relevance: A moderator excuse needs its own test. When a check fails, cite the failing output (G2), not a story.

source: Errington et al. (2021) Challenges for assessing replicability in preclinical cancer biology
finding: Cancer biology replications were hard to start because original papers lacked the information to repeat them.
numbers: 193 experiments from 53 papers selected; 50 experiments from 23 papers completed. Raw data public for 4 (2%); obtained for 31 (16%); nothing for 131 (68%). Statistics reported for 78 of 193 (40%). No experiment needed zero protocol clarifications; 20% needed strong or extreme help (15% strong, 5% extreme). Authors not helpful or silent for 32%. Mean cost $52,574 per replication.
quote: Raw data was publicly accessible for just 2% of experiments to reproduce the findings.
limits: Only the first 100,000 of about 450,000 characters read. High-impact papers only.
agent_relevance: Method must be written so another party can rerun it. Log the full protocol, seeds and raw outputs for every test.

source: Errington et al. (2021) Investigating the replicability of preclinical cancer biology
finding: Preclinical cancer effects shrank by 85% on replication.
numbers: 158 effects (136 positive, 22 null); 97 positive effects with tests. Median effect size original 2.96, replication 0.43 (85% smaller); 92% of replication effects smaller. Same direction and p<.05: 42/97 (43%). Original ES inside replication CI: 17 (18%). Replication ES inside original CI: 42 (43%). Meta-analysis p<.05: 60 (62%). Three or more of five criteria: 39/97 (40%).
quote: The median effect size in the replications was 85% smaller than the median effect size in the original experiments.
limits: The verdict depends on the rule (18% to 62%). Only first 100,000 of 274,741 characters read.
agent_relevance: Fix the pass rule before running a test; the verdict changes with the rule. Keep the rule in code (G5).

source: Franklin and Perovic, Stanford Encyclopedia: Experiment in Physics (Franklin's epistemology of experiment)
finding: Seven strategies physicists use to argue an observation is real; none is infallible.
numbers: Strategies: intervention; independent confirmation; calibration against known phenomena (e.g. Balmer series); reproducing known artifacts; eliminating plausible error sources (Sherlock Holmes); results too consistent to be artifact; explanation by well-corroborated theory; apparatus based on corroborated theory; statistical arguments. The three-sigma bump rule was raised to four sigma after look-elsewhere concerns.
limits: Philosophy review, not a measured study. Only the first 100,000 characters read. Year is of the current SEP revision as I could not confirm it.
agent_relevance: Maps onto S4 test design: calibrate the checker on known cases, run an artifact control, list error sources, add an independent route, set a chance threshold that counts the search.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia: Experiment in Physics, Weber gravity waves and Collins's experimenter's regress
finding: Collins: a good apparatus is one giving the right answer, and no rule breaks the circle. The SEP reply: in Weber's case concrete checks did.
numbers: Six other groups reported nulls. Critics shared data and analysis code, reanalysed with Weber's nonlinear algorithm and still saw nothing, and calibrated detectors with pulses of known energy and saw them. Weber's apparatus did not detect the calibration pulses. Weber had an admitted programming error that made spurious coincidences.
limits: SEP argues one side; Collins disputes that the nulls count as replications. No counts of the regress itself.
agent_relevance: Break a test-trust regress with known-signal injection and shared code. Plant a positive before trusting a null, and a null before trusting a positive.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia: Experiment in Physics, Galison and Hacking
finding: Galison: experiments end when the result would stand up in court; image-tradition groups trust single golden events, logic-tradition groups trust statistics. Hacking: intervention and independent confirmation support belief.
numbers: Hacking: the same dot pattern across different microscopes is unlikely an artifact; stable lab science is mutually self-vindicating between theory and equipment (1992). Staley (1999) disputes Galison's split and says both traditions use statistical argument.
limits: Historical claims, no quantified test. Staley dispute unresolved here.
agent_relevance: Two stopping rules exist, one vivid case or many-case statistics. For the agent, one clean case is not proof (G3); require independent routes.

source: Beel and Kan (2025) Evaluating Sakana's AI Scientist for autonomous research
finding: An independent test of an automated experiment pipeline found weak execution and unsound reporting.
numbers: 5 of 12 proposed experiments (42%) failed from coding errors. Each revision added only 8% more characters on average. Median 5 citations per paper; only 5 of 34 citations from 2020 or later. 4 of 7 manuscripts (57%) had incorrect or hallucinated numbers. An energy-saving experiment reported accuracy gains while using more compute, contradicting its goal.
quote: Hallucinated numerical results were contained in several manuscripts, undermining the reliability of its outputs.
limits: Small run (12 ideas, 7 manuscripts), recommender-systems domain, v1 templates, consumer laptop.
agent_relevance: Code that runs is not a design that tests the claim. Check the stated goal against logged output (G2, G10).

source: Beel and Kan (2025) novelty check by keyword search
finding: The tool's literature check was keyword matching, so known ideas passed as new.
numbers: Micro-batching for SGD and other established ideas were labelled novel. The tool marked 10 generated ideas and both seed ideas as novel. Only the binary label feeds the workflow; other scores looked arbitrary.
limits: Same small sample. The tool sometimes flagged non-novel in earlier tests.
agent_relevance: Supports G8: novelty by running and real search, not by model self-rating.

source: Starace et al. (2025) PaperBench
finding: Agents must rebuild a paper's code and rerun its results. Best agent reached 21% under a basic scaffold.
numbers: 20 ICML 2024 papers, 8,316 gradable outcomes, rubrics co-developed with authors. BasicAgent: Claude 3.5 Sonnet (New) 21.0%, o1 13.2%, others under 10%. IterativeAgent (cannot quit early): o1-high 24.4%, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 16.1%, o3-mini-high 8.5%. 36-hour o1 run 26.0%. Code-Dev variant (no execution) o1 43.4%.
limits: LLM judge grades; judge F1 about 0.83 on auxiliary set. Scaffold changed the ranking (Claude fell, o1 rose).
agent_relevance: Getting results to match is the hard part: 43.4% code-only vs about 24 to 26% with execution. Agents stop early; forcing continuation helped some models and hurt others (G7).

source: Starace et al. (2025) PaperBench human baseline
finding: ML PhDs beat the model once they had enough time, but the model led early.
numbers: 8 ML PhD participants, 3 independent attempts per paper, best of 3. On a 3-paper subset humans 41.4% after 48 hours vs o1 26.6%. o1 led in the first hours, humans overtook after about 24 hours; o1 plateaued after the first hour.
quote: humans start outperforming the AI agent after 24 hours
limits: Small human sample; best-of-3 inflates the human score; a few runs used an A100 instead of an A10.
agent_relevance: The agent writes a lot fast and then stalls. A stall should trigger a re-plan (G1) and later time should go to checking, not more code.

source: Siegel et al. (2024) CORE-Bench: computational reproducibility agent benchmark
finding: Reproducing a paper's results from supplied code and data is hard for agents. A tailored scaffold helped a lot.
numbers: 90 papers from CodeOcean, 270 tasks, three difficulty levels. CORE-Agent GPT-4o: Easy 60.00%, Medium 57.78%, Hard 21.48%. GPT-4o-mini: 44.44, 32.59, 16.30. AutoGPT GPT-4o: 35.56, 37.78, 6.67. Task-specific scaffold raised Hard from 6.7% to 21.5%.
limits: Pass@1 on test split; CORE-Agent run 3 times, AutoGPT once. Curated CodeOcean capsules only.
agent_relevance: Same model, a scaffold aimed at the failure tripled hard-task accuracy. Supports G7 when the scaffold targets the failure.

source: Siegel et al. (2024) CORE-Bench Table 1: human reproducibility with code and data shared
finding: Human science often fails to reproduce even when code and data are shared.
numbers: ML reproducibility challenge 2022: only 18 of 28 papers fully reproducible; 6 of 28 not fully reproduced even after talking to authors. Table also lists Hardwicke 2021 (psychology, 25 studies), Gertler 2018 (economics, 203), Belz 2021 (NLP, 549), Prignon 2024 (finance, 1008); the column labels were garbled in extraction, so those counts are not used.
limits: Secondary compilation. Only the ML figure was read cleanly.
agent_relevance: Even a pass with code and data is not guaranteed to repeat. Record environment, seeds and versions.

source: Huang et al. (2024) MLAgentBench: language agents for machine learning experimentation
finding: A GPT-4 research agent that runs ML experiments succeeded on 37.5% of 13 tasks on average, with huge spread.
numbers: 13 tasks. Average success 37.5%. 100% on house-price training over 8 runs. 0 to 25% on recent Kaggle and BabyLM tasks. Success defined as beating the baseline by 10% or more.
limits: Success is beating a baseline, not scientific validity. Older tasks may be partly memorised.
agent_relevance: Familiar tasks hide weakness. Test on tasks newer than the model cutoff (G3).

source: Chen et al. (2025) ScienceAgentBench: data-driven scientific discovery
finding: Data-driven discovery tasks from 44 papers: the best agent solved about a third unaided.
numbers: 102 tasks from 44 peer-reviewed papers in 4 disciplines, checked by 9 experts. Best agent 32.4% independently, 34.3% with expert-provided knowledge. o1 reasoning raised success to 42.2% at much higher cost. Three attempts per task. Two contamination strategies used.
limits: Single-program tasks, not whole experiments.
agent_relevance: Expert hints added under 2 points, so the gap is skill with data, not missing knowledge. Spend by difficulty (G12).

source: MLE-bench (2025): machine learning engineering agents on 75 Kaggle competitions
finding: Best agent earned at least a bronze medal in 16.9% of competitions; more attempts doubled that.
numbers: o1-preview with AIDE: 16.9% pass@1, 34.1% pass@8. GPT-4o 8.7% with 24 hours, 11.8% with 100 hours. Agents do well on known methods and struggle to debug and recover from missteps. Plagiarism checks and contamination tests included.
limits: Kaggle medal is the target, not new science.
agent_relevance: Several attempts doubled success, but G4 says samples are correlated, so the gain needs a real selector such as a held-out score.

source: Sakana AI team (2025) The AI Scientist-v2: workshop-level discovery via agentic tree search
finding: Of three fully AI-written papers sent to an ICLR workshop, one was above the acceptance bar.
numbers: 3 manuscripts; one scored 6.33 (6, 6, 7), about top 45%; the other two were not accepted. The paper was withdrawn after review by prior agreement; reviewers were told after. The authors' own review: none met main-track standards. The accepted paper reported a negative result on compositional regularisation.
quote: one manuscript achieved an average reviewer score of 6.33
limits: One success in three, workshop level, authors chose what to submit, nodes picked by an LLM. Not a replication.
agent_relevance: Tree search with repeated runs of the best node is a design to copy, but pick winners by run output, not by LLM judge (G5, G8).

source: Aher, Arriaga, Kalai (2023) Using LLMs to simulate multiple humans and replicate human subject studies
finding: Four classic experiments were simulated with LLMs. Three replicated and one showed a distortion.
numbers: Ultimatum Game, Garden Path sentences and Milgram replicated with recent models. Wisdom of Crowds showed hyper-accuracy: ChatGPT and GPT-4 simulated participants had median 1.0 with IQR 0.0 on general-knowledge questions. In the largest model a majority gave exactly correct answers to all 10 questions.
limits: Simulated subjects; training data may hold these classics, so replication may be recall.
agent_relevance: Using a model as a stand-in subject pool gives falsely tidy data. Do not treat model samples as independent (G4).

source: Aher et al. (2023) hyper-accuracy: bigger models, narrower crowds
finding: Larger, more aligned models give less varied answers than a real crowd, which erases the wisdom-of-crowds effect.
numbers: Human comparison study had 52 subjects (Moussaid et al. 2013). Earlier GPT models did not show the distortion; it grew with size and alignment across 6 models. 10 questions (5 reused, 5 new).
limits: Alignment as cause is a hypothesis, not tested directly.
agent_relevance: Supports G4: samples from one model collapse onto one answer, so agreement means little.
